title: Guests as Christ
hookLine: the Rule of Benedict: let all guests be received as Christ (Rule 53)

cards: A knock at the monastery gate, after dark. Rain. On the other side of the door, a stranger: muddy boots, a wet cloak, nobody the porter has ever seen.
Could be a pilgrim. Could be a thief. Could be a lord in disguise, or a beggar with nowhere else to go.
The old porter gets up from his bench by the gate, and the words he's been taught come out first, before any question about who this is: thanks be to God.

teach.b: The Rule of Benedict, the guidebook for monks from yesterday, has a chapter on guests, and it opens with a startling instruction: let every guest who comes be received as Christ. Why?

teach.h: I WAS A STRANGER, AND YE TOOK ME IN.
teach.b: Because, the Rule says, Christ himself will one day say the words of Matthew's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." So the stranger at the gate isn't an interruption.
In the Rule's eyes, the stranger is Christ, arriving in disguise. And the chapter gets specific. The superior and the brothers go out to meet the guest.
They pray together, then exchange the kiss of peace.

teach.h: WATER, FEET, BREAD, THE POOR FIRST.
teach.b: The abbot pours water over the guest's hands, and he and the community wash the guest's feet. Visitors are fed.
The Rule adds a line that's easy to miss: the poor and pilgrims are to be shown the most care, because in them Christ is received more especially.

The rich, it notes dryly, get respect anyway, because people are wary of them. It's practical too. The abbot and the guests have their own kitchen, so people arriving at all hours don't disturb the brothers.

The first letter of Peter puts the same welcome in a few plain words: "Use hospitality one to another without grudging." Without grudging, even at the door after dark. The idea underneath doesn't need a monastery.
Every door, sooner or later, has a stranger on the other side.

how: Benedictine monasteries and convents keep guest houses where visitors can stay, pray with the community and share meals, and the porter or guest master greets them in the spirit of Rule 53.

games.q: you're the porter of a monastery. a stranger knocks after dark: muddy, soaked, unknown. what does the Rule have you do first?
o: ask who they are and what they want.
greet them with thanks to God and receive them as Christ.
tell them to come back in the morning.
games.why: the Rule has the brothers go out to meet the guest and receive them as Christ, with the poor and pilgrims shown the most care.

practice: Think of the people who'll come to your door today, in person, on a screen, in your inbox: a coworker who always needs something, a delivery driver, a child who interrupts, someone you'd rather avoid.
Choose one, and picture them arriving, and yourself standing up and going to meet them, glad they came. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just hold them in mind kindly.
